title: ADHD time blindness: why cleaning feels like forever
description: You avoid the kitchen because it feels like an hour. ADHD time blindness makes cleaning feel huge, but time it once and it's six minutes, not willpower.
h1: Why cleaning feels like it takes forever with ADHD (and the six-minute fix)
target_query: why does cleaning feel like it takes forever with ADHD

faq.q: Why do tasks feel like they take forever with ADHD?
faq.a: ADHD brains have trouble sensing how much time a task will actually take, so a short job gets a huge estimate. That is time blindness. The feeling is real, but the number your brain hands you is usually wrong, and it is what makes you avoid the task.

faq.q: How long does cleaning the kitchen actually take?
faq.a: Most of the daily reset jobs you dread, wiping the counter, loading the dishwasher, clearing the sink, take between three and ten minutes. Wiping a counter is often under two. The only way to trust this is to time yourself once so you have your own real number instead of the inflated one.

faq.q: Is avoiding chores an ADHD thing or just laziness?
faq.a: It is an ADHD thing. Avoidance is a predictable response to a task that feels enormous, and time blindness is what makes it feel enormous. You are not choosing to dodge a six-minute job, you are dodging the two-hour version your brain invented. Shrink the estimate and the avoidance eases.

sources.supports: Altered time perception is a clinically relevant feature of ADHD.
Time perception problems are a focal symptom of adult ADHD, so estimates of task length run wrong.
